lead: Japanese ukiyo-e artist (1760-1849) from Edo; known for woodblock prints in which a few flat colors, first indigo, then Prussian blue, carry the picture.
paras: Katsushika Hokusai worked in Edo, now Tokyo, across more than six decades and under many names. His series of views of Mount Fuji, begun around 1830, made him known outside Japan.

The blue in those prints matters. Prussian blue, called Bero-ai in Japan, reached Japan through Dutch and Chinese trade in the 1820s, and Hokusai's Fuji series is often cited as an early major use. It sits beside older indigo and spreads from pale to deep in a single print.
Prints from woodblocks use a small set of flat inks, one block per color. Each impression of the same design can differ in how the inks were mixed and how much they have faded since.
Check the paper. In a worn impression the sky and the paper often meet at a pale cream; faded ink and toned paper change the picture.

Our archive holds 335 Hokusai works, photographs and scans of paper and silk, not pigment tests. His strongest signatures are paper tones: Beige, in 46 of 335 works at over five times the usual rate, plus Olive-Buff, Stone and Putty. He used dark olive browns and Smoky Black far less than peers, which fits color printing with light grounds.
